Two railroads tripled his shipping price. He didn't pay it.

They thought they had him — no pipeline, no other way to move the oil, pay up or shut down. He walked his refinery instead, looking for what he was already throwing away.

He built his own pipe next to their tracks. One-tenth the cost, forever. Every adversity carries the seed of a bigger win hidden inside it — you just have to walk around long enough to find it.

You can do everything right and still never get the money.

It's not always the plan that's broken. Sometimes it's a belief that was never yours to begin with — a grandmother's fear, a camel through the eye of a needle, a lesson that the rich don't go to heaven. It gets passed down in the DNA and in the silence, long before you ever formed an opinion about money yourself.

You can't manifest past a block you don't know is there. The first step is finding whose voice it actually is.

Magicians have been saying the real secret out loud this whole time.

Abracadabra isn't nonsense. It comes from ancient Persian, and it translates to "I now create with my words." Every tradition says some version of it — you're hung by your own tongue, snared by the words of your mouth.

Most people use that power by accident, narrating their own limits out loud all day. Once you hear it this way, you can't unhear the words you've been feeding yourself.

Every success book tells you to be grateful first. That's the part that's missing a step.

He's spent decades around people with nine figures in the bank, and not one of them walks around in quiet appreciation. They get angry. They get specific about what they will not tolerate anymore, before they ever clarify what they actually want.

You don't live in that anger, you visit it — just long enough to know what you're done accepting. Only then does gratitude belong in the sequence.

#manifestation #mindset #awakening #lawofattraction #success #kevintrudeau

Michael Jordan missed more game-winning shots than any player in history.

Not the highest percentage. Not even close. He just always said the same four words: give me the ball. The attitude came first, every single time, win or miss — and the makes piled up because he never once stopped asking for the shot.

Winning isn't the goal for people like that. Losing is just unacceptable. That's a different engine entirely, and it runs on wanting it more than it runs on being good at it.
